entries.body: A real person at a real company with a legitimate sales request that passed pre-check.
A lead the owning rep has accepted after the QL to SAL decision (step 2b).
Not ready now; returned to nurture with a reason and a re-entry trigger.

entries.rationale: Pre-check runs before research so the lead lands with the right person instead of being worked cold.

entries.body:
Routing happens after the lead is triaged, and it decides whose meeting link goes in the email.
An account owned by an AE in HubSpot is left to HubSpot's workflow, whatever its class. Otherwise a good fit for enterprise goes to an AE: the Commercial AE at 8,000 employees or fewer, else the next Enterprise AE in the round robin (the Commercial accounts block). The email carries the AE's meeting link to speed up the sales process.
A lead the PA thinks has potential, but that is not an enterprise fit yet, is the PA's call: the email carries the PA's own meeting link.
Anything unclear qualifies first with questions and no link. The PA can change the route on any lead.
entries.rationale: Fred, 2026-09-30: the lead is routed from the PA to the AE once it meets the enterprise bar; otherwise the PA takes the call.

entries.body:
A commercial account is a company with max_employees employees or fewer.
Owned by an AE in HubSpot, whatever the class or size: nothing happens in PA. HubSpot's own workflow emails them, so there is no draft, no decision, and no SLA.
Not owned by an AE, max_employees employees or fewer: route to the Commercial AE.
Not owned by an AE, more than max_employees employees: round robin to the next Enterprise AE. The pick is saved, so the lead keeps its AE.
An unknown employee count goes to the enterprise round robin and is flagged to check.
The Commercial AE and the Enterprise AEs are set in Settings, Organization, under Lead routing.
entries.rationale: Fred, 2026-10-01: 8k or less and unowned by an AE goes to the Commercial AE; 8k+ and unowned round robins to an Enterprise AE. Owned by an AE: nothing happens in PA; HubSpot's workflow emails them.

entries.source: Sales handbook, 03 Lead routing: Contact Sales responds within 30 minutes

entries.rationale: Size the buying entity. For an agency buying for an unnamed client, enterprise fit is unknown until the client is named.

entries.body:
Every Contact Sales lead is Exceptional or Requires discovery, from five signals. Agencies take the agency path first.
Exceptional (route to the AE) when at least exceptional_signals of these are true. Intent score (HubSpot Company Fit Score, Breeze, 0 to 10) of intent_exceptional or more. A clear enterprise need in the inbound message. employees_exceptional or more employees. A clearly defined budget (the form says Approved, or the message names one; may need outside research). Multiple sign-ups from the account (HubSpot company, Number of Associated Sign Up Contacts, at least signups_multiple).
Requires discovery (qualify first) otherwise. Typically an intent score of 2 to 5, a potential or unclear enterprise need, an unknown budget, under 100 employees, and a single sign-up.
An intent score of intent_recycle or less suggests a recycle, and no intent score counts as 0. Those leads get one email asking them to clarify, not a sequence. The PA decides.
Content or Code only picks the email angle and the questions.
entries.rationale: Fred, 2026-10-01: exceptional leads route to the AE; anything less requires discovery.

entries.body:
Every first touch follows TCQ, and every draft is checked against it.
Answer what they asked first. If they asked for a call, a demo, pricing, or a plan, the email says yes and how it happens before anything else. Never skip their ask to ask your own questions.
Trigger. Open on the specific thing they said, in their words, from the message or a form answer (business driver, how they will measure success, budget status, who makes the call, tech stack, use case). Never "thanks for reaching out about Builder" as the whole trigger, never a paraphrase that loses their detail. The exact words quoted go in rubric.trigger; PA checks they appear in the form and in the email.
Connection. One short, plain line that shows you understood their setup, using their specifics (their stack, languages, team, what they already have). Not a lesson about their situation and not a generalization ("teams like yours usually find", "the hard part is"); skip it rather than lecture. Never a feature list, "Builder can help teams", or "our platform". Goes in rubric.connection.
Question. The ask. At most two questions, the ones that matter most for the call or the next step, or the time offer. Reasonable, 15 to 30 minutes, never "demo our platform". Goes in rubric.ask.
Classify the lead first, then follow the formula for its class (the class blocks below).
Under 75 words when possible. No filler like "I'll confirm the best-fit approach and get back to you"; only promise to confirm something real they asked that you cannot answer.
The lead's route decides the ask (the Routing section; get-engagement returns it as leadRoute). Route to the AE, or the PA takes the call, means that person's meeting link is the ask, exactly as given, with no day suggestions. Route to the AE also loops the AE in: they are on CC, named in the email, and the email says what the meeting is for. Qualify first and the agency path carry no link yet.
Never disclose pricing, except the Content price check. Never invent a fact, metric, headcount, quote, or customer result. A qualifying question is not fabrication.

banned_phrases: I hope this email finds you well
Would you be open to a quick call

entries.source: xDR master instructions (V2 messaging) and the TCQ email framework

entries.body:
A technical founder or staff engineer, plain and a little casual. Helpful, not preachy: no lessons, no telling them what their problem really is, no restating their message back at length.
No em dashes, no colons, no "Best regards". A casual sign-off, signed with the owner's first name.
Say Builder, never Builder.io, Fusion, or Publish. Write in the prospect's language.
"Design-to-code" may describe their problem, never the pitch. Win on collaboration and control, not on out-coding Cursor or Copilot.
At most one proof point, and only from the Sales handbook's approved customer evidence.
Never pitch a demo as the first call; call it an intro, walkthrough, or working session.
Ambiguous domains (student, personal, generic) are a yellow flag, not a disqualifier. A Contact Sales form is intent, so write a qualifying first touch that surfaces the team and company, and flag the domain in the brief.
entries.source: xDR master instructions (V2 messaging) and the TCQ email framework

entries.body:
Fill the biggest gap, and only after answering what they asked. At most two questions. Ask about their pain and their world, never their interest in us or their buying process.
Never ask "what's driving your interest", "who signs off", "want to see a demo", "do you have 15 minutes", or "what's your traffic".
The test. With every mention of Builder removed, would a thoughtful peer ask this?
Do not re-ask what the message or the form already answered.
entries.source: xDR master instructions (V2 messaging) and the TCQ email framework

entries.body:
Exceptional, Content.
Routed to the AE, who is looped in (PA adds them on CC). Answer what they asked and acknowledge the initiative in their words. One sentence that the CMS is part of the Enterprise plan.
Introduce the AE by name and suggest the meeting with the intention behind it, in their terms (for example, to map their sites and editors onto the Enterprise setup and walk through pricing). Then the AE's meeting link, clearly, on its own line. At most one question, only for a genuine gap.
entries.source: xDR master instructions (V2 messaging) and the TCQ email framework

entries.body:
Requires discovery, Content.
Acknowledge in their words. One line that the CMS is part of the Enterprise plan. Ask 2 or 3 of the Content questions the message and form have not answered (how many pages, who edits, current setup, page types, timeline). No demo on the first touch; conversation first.
Qualify first by default, so no link. When the PA takes the call, end with the PA's meeting link after the questions.
entries.source: xDR master instructions (V2 messaging) and the TCQ email framework

entries.body:
Content price check.
Only in reply to a pricing ask on a clearly small lead (both employees under 50 and page views under 500k are known). Give the anchor from the Sales handbook, hedged. Otherwise no pricing.
entries.source: xDR master instructions (V2 messaging) and the TCQ email framework

entries.body:
Exceptional, Code.
Routed to the AE, who is looped in (PA adds them on CC). Answer what they asked, then introduce the AE by name and suggest the meeting with the intention behind it, in their terms (for example, to look at how their design system and codebase would work with Builder). Then the AE's meeting link, clearly, on its own line. At most one prep question, led by a hypothesis anchored in V2 pain (work rebuilt at handoff, AI gains not compounding), followed by "or is there a different challenge driving this?". Prefer questions that double as signals (is engineering in the loop, Cursor or Copilot, SSO, seats).

entries.body:
Requires discovery, Code.
Acknowledge, a line of value, 2 or 3 qualifying questions (enterprise signals, a path to engineering), then "let me know and we can find time". Company size alone never decides enterprise need.
Qualify first by default, so no link. When the PA takes the call, end with the PA's meeting link instead.

entries.body:
Agency, SI, or consultancy. Partner framing first.
Find the path. Internal use, a client project, or exploring.
For a client project, ask the client's headcount and HQ before proposing times. Offer the partner path when relevant.
Routing and who to route to are in the Sales handbook (03).

One clarification email.
For a lead that suggests a recycle (no intent score, or 0 to 1). One short email, not a sequence and no meeting link.
Thank them, answer anything they asked in a line (a call or pricing can be set up once it is clear what they need), then ask one or two questions that clarify who they are and what they want to do with Builder.
Under 60 words. If they do not reply, the lead recycles.

A bad draft and a better one (Requires discovery, Content).
Their message. "We need a CMS so marketing can run the whole site in English and Arabic (right to left) without a developer, with an approval step before anything goes live. We already have a bilingual React site. We'd like to discuss the Enterprise plan, a demo on a bilingual site, and pricing. Could we book a call?"

Bad. "Saw you want marketing running the whole site day to day, in English and Arabic RTL, without pulling in a developer. Teams like yours usually find that once that eng dependency lifts, the hard part is keeping brand consistent. The CMS you're describing is part of our Enterprise plan. How many pages does marketing publish a month? Who's doing that work today? What's your rough timeline?"
Why it is bad. It ignores the call, the demo, and pricing they asked for. It restates their message and lectures them about their own problem. Three questions read like an interrogation.

Better.
Hi Sam,

Happy to set up a call. We can walk through a bilingual demo with Arabic right to left and approvals before publish, and cover the Enterprise plan and pricing there.

Since you already run a React site, is the plan to keep it and add the CMS on top, or rebuild? I'll send times once I hear back.

Riley
